items.prose: An arm's running mean is 0.55 after 20 rewards. The 21st reward is 1.
items.question: What is the new estimate? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use old + step × error with step $\tfrac{1}{21}$.

byKey.twentieth: You used a step of $\tfrac{1}{20}$. This is the 21st reward.
byKey.full: You took the whole error. The step is $\tfrac{1}{21}$.
byKey.average: You averaged 0.55 and 1 as if they were two rewards. 0.55 already stands for 20.

explain.text: The error is $1 - 0.55 = 0.45$, and a 21st of it is 0.0214. So the estimate rises to 0.5714, the mean of 12 wins in 21.

items.prose: Three strategies earn a hit with chance 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7. An agent tried them 100, 250 and 650 times.
items.question: What is the expected regret of this record?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply each strategy's count by its gap to 0.7.

byKey.reward: That is the expected number of hits. Regret is the shortfall against $1000 \times 0.7 = 700$.
byKey.one-arm: You counted only the worst strategy. The middle one trails by 0.2.
byKey.to-mean: You used the middle strategy's count alone. Add the worst strategy's 40.

explain.text: The gaps are 0.4, 0.2 and 0. So regret is $100 \times 0.4 + 250 \times 0.2 = 90$ hits.

items.prose: Epsilon-greedy with $\varepsilon = 0.05$ runs for 5,000 pulls on arms with win chances 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7.
items.question: What is the least regret its random pulls can cost over the 5,000 pulls?

feedback.generic: Not quite. A random pull loses the average gap; count the random pulls.

byKey.per-pull: That is the floor per pull. Multiply by 5,000.
byKey.no-eps: You charged every pull. Only 1 in 20 is random.
byKey.worst: You used the worst arm's gap, 0.4. A uniform random pull loses the average gap, 0.2.

explain.text: The mean value is 0.5, so a random pull loses 0.2 on average. About 250 pulls are random, so the floor is $250 \times 0.2 = 50$.

items.prose: A venue's estimate is 0.8. It is tracked with a constant step $\alpha = 0.3$. The next two orders do not fill.
items.question: What is the estimate after both? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply $Q + 0.3(R - Q)$ twice with $R = 0$.

byKey.one: That is after one miss. Apply the update again.
byKey.mean: You averaged 0.8, 0 and 0. A constant step keeps 70% of the old estimate each time.
byKey.double: You took $0.3 \times 2 = 0.6$ off at once. Each update keeps 70% of what is there.

explain.text: Each miss keeps $1 - 0.3 = 0.7$ of the estimate. So it falls to $0.8 \times 0.7^2 = 0.392$.

items.prose: At pull $t = 200$ an agent running UCB1 has the record below. $2\ln 200 = 10.5966$.
items.question: Which arm does UCB1 pull next?

options.why: Arm 2 has the best estimate, but its 70 pulls give a bonus of only 0.3891. Arm 3 scores 1.5351.
Arm 1 has the most pulls, so the smallest bonus: it scores 0.8172.

options.text: It needs a random draw to decide
options.why: UCB1 is deterministic: it pulls the largest score.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add each arm's bonus to its estimate.

explain.text: The scores are 0.8172, 0.9991 and 1.5351. Arm 3's 9 pulls earn a bonus of 1.0851, so it gets the pull.

items.prose: You want the mean of $n$ rewards in $[0, 1]$ to exceed its true value by 0.05 or more with chance at most 0.01, by Hoeffding's one-sided bound.
items.question: What is the smallest $n$ that guarantees it?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Solve $e^{-2n\varepsilon^2} = 0.01$ for $n$ and round up.

byKey.cheb: That is Chebyshev's $\tfrac{1}{4n\varepsilon^2} \le 0.01$, which bounds both tails and is looser.
byKey.two: You used the two-sided bound $2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$. The question asks about exceeding only.
byKey.no-two: You dropped the 2 in the exponent: $\ln 100 / 0.0025$.

explain.text: Taking logs, $2n \times 0.0025 \ge \ln 100 = 4.6052$, so $n \ge 921.03$. The smallest whole $n$ is 922.

items.prose: From $\mathrm{Beta}(1, 1)$ priors, venue A has filled 4 of 5 orders and venue B 40 of 70.
items.question: How does Thompson sampling treat the two venues on the next pull?

options.text: It usually pulls A, but B still wins some draws
It always pulls A, whose posterior mean is higher
options.why: Thompson pulls the larger draw, not the larger mean. B's narrow posterior sometimes beats a draw from A's wide one.

options.text: It usually pulls B, the venue with more evidence
options.why: Evidence narrows B's curve but does not raise it. A's mean, 0.7143, is above B's 0.5694.

options.text: It splits the pulls evenly until both have 70 orders
options.why: Thompson never balances counts on purpose. It pulls each venue with the chance that it is best.

feedback.correct: A's draw beats B's with chance 0.8007 (by integration): usually, not always.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how often a draw from A's posterior beats one from B's.

explain.text: A is $\mathrm{Beta}(5, 2)$, mean 0.7143; B is $\mathrm{Beta}(41, 31)$, mean 0.5694. A's draw is the larger with chance 0.8007, so A gets most pulls and B the rest.

items.prose: A venue gets the prior $\mathrm{Beta}(3, 7)$, then fills all of its first 10 orders.
items.question: What is its posterior mean? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add 10 wins to the first parameter.

byKey.data: That is the data alone. The prior still counts as 10 orders, 3 of them fills.
byKey.prior: That is the prior mean before any orders.
byKey.swap: You added the fills to the second parameter.

explain.text: Ten fills make it $\mathrm{Beta}(3 + 10, 7)$, mean $\tfrac{13}{20} = 0.65$. The prior pulls the estimate halfway from 1 down to 0.3.

items.prose: A greedy agent starts every estimate at 1, counted as one pretend win, on three arms.
items.question: Why does it beat plain greedy started at 0?

options.text: Untried arms keep a score of 1, so it tries every arm before settling
It explores at random until the pretend wins wear off
options.why: No random pulls happen. It picks the best estimate, and an untried arm still shows 1.

options.text: It learns each arm's value faster
options.why: Each estimate learns at the same rate. The gain is that every arm gets tried.

options.text: Its estimates end up closer to the true values
options.why: The pretend win biases the estimates upwards a little. The gain is in which arms get tried.

feedback.correct: Optimism makes every untried arm look best, so each gets a pull or more.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what an untried arm's estimate is.

explain.text: After a loss an arm's estimate falls below 1, while untried arms still show 1. So greedy moves on and tries them all. Over seeds 0 to 199 regret fell from 61.8 to 27.9.

items.prose: Run each agent for a very long horizon $T$ on arms with different values.
items.question: Which agent's regret keeps growing in proportion to $T$?

options.why: UCB1's regret grows like $\ln T$: its bonus shrinks on a worse arm as it is pulled.
Thompson's pulls of a worse arm thin out as its posterior narrows, so regret grows like $\ln T$.

options.text: Epsilon-greedy with $\varepsilon_t$ falling to 0 at a suitable rate
options.why: A suitably falling rate removes the fixed floor. That is why it is used.

feedback.correct: A fixed $\varepsilon$ pays $\varepsilon(q^* - \bar q)$ on every pull for ever.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which rule never stops exploring at the same rate?

explain.text: Fixed epsilon-greedy pays the floor $\varepsilon(q^* - \bar q)$ per pull, so its regret grows like $T$. UCB1 and Thompson grow like $\ln T$, even if UCB1 takes long to overtake.
